items.title: Turn Jira tickets into GitLab merge requests with Duo Agent Platform
items.summary: Many teams plan in Jira and ship in GitLab. Even if you already use GitLab Duo Agent Platform, you still open Jira to read each ticket, copy it into an agent for implementation, and report the merge request back.This tutorial shows you how to remove that handoff. You add a Jira agent to Duo Agentic Chat. The agent knows your project and repository, and you use it to find, create, and update tickets. Then you hand a ticket to Developer Flow with /goal, and Developer Flow creates the merge request.Watch the short demo first: A custom Jira agent finds the urgent tickets, one goes to Developer Flow, and the merge request shows up on the Jira ticket.PrerequisitesGitLab Premium or Ultimate on GitLab.com, with GitLab Duo Agent Platform turned on for your top-level group and Developer Flow enabled for the project.For the Atlassian MCP server in the AI Catalog: experiment and beta features turned on for the top-level group (Settings > GitLab Duo > Change configuration).Maintainer or Owner role on the project for the one-time settings in Steps 1 and 2; Developer or above on a project to use the agent there afterwards.A Jira Cloud project you can read and comment on, and Atlassian admin access once, to trust GitLab as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. Jira names a ticket with a ticket key: the project key plus a number. Our examples use project key KAN, so an example ticket key looks like KAN-123. The examples also use GitLab project my-group/my-project.A Jira API token from id.atlassian.com, used only by GitLab's Jira integration in Step 1.Note: The Atlassian MCP server in the AI Catalog is an experiment and isn't ready for production use. Try it on a test project first.TutorialHere are the steps to follow to turn Jira tickets into GitLab merge requests.1. Connect GitLab to JiraThis is GitLab's standard Jira integration. It makes any MR that mentions a ticket, for example KAN-123, show up on that Jira ticket, and posts a comment there. Five minutes, done once per project.In GitLab, open the project and go to Settings > Integrations > Jira issues.Select Active.Web URL: your Jira site, for example https://your-site.atlassian.net.Authentication: Basic. Enter your Atlassian email and the API token.Under Trigger, select Commit and Merge request, and tick Enable comments.Optional: under Jira issues, tick View Jira issues and enter KAN. You get a Jira issue list inside GitLab under Plan > Jira issues.Test settings, then Save changes.Reference: Jira issue integration.2. Create the Jira custom agentGitLab Duo Agent Platform lets you create custom agents right in the UI. Give the agent a name, a prompt, and tools through an MCP server. We'll call ours Jira, with a prompt tuned for triage, summaries, and ticket hygiene, and the Atlassian MCP server for the tools to act on Jira.Setup takes about 10 minutes: create the agent once, enable it in any project that needs it, and each person connects their own Atlassian account in Step 2.3. Creating the agent publishes it to the AI Catalog automatically. In its configuration you choose the managing project, and only Maintainers and Owners of that project can edit the agent. Deleting an agent requires an administrator. Its visibility decides which projects can enable it: a Private agent can't be shared with other projects, a Restricted agent can be used by anyone in the managing project's top-level group, and a Public agent can be viewed and used by anyone. Creating an agent does not make it available anywhere, though: You enable it separately in each project that should use it, including the managing project, in Step 2.2 Section 5.2.1. Let Atlassian trust GitLabGo to admin.atlassian.com and pick the organization that owns your Jira site (if you have more than one, the right org lists your Jira site under Apps > Atlassian apps). In the left sidebar, select Connectors > Atlassian MCP server, then Add domain and enter https://gitlab.com/**. You need Atlassian organization admin rights for this page. Without it, the OAuth step in 2.3 fails because Atlassian refuses GitLab as an MCP client. Reference: Control Atlassian MCP server settings.2.2. Create the custom agentIn GitLab, open your project and select AI > Agents > New agent.Name: Jira. Description: Ask about Jira tickets, triage, summarize, comment, and hand work to the Developer flowSystem prompt:You are the team's Jira assistant inside GitLab. You answer anything about Jira work for thisproject using the Jira tools; you never guess ticket contents.Triage: when asked what is urgent, open, blocked or due, search with JQL and answer with a shorttable: key, summary, priority, status, assignee, days open. Default to the current user's openissues in the project unless they say otherwise. Offer one follow-up filter.Summaries: when asked about a ticket, fetch it with its comments and linked issues, and give therequirement in a few lines plus any open questions from the comments.
